title: Pronouns
summary: The personal pronouns in every case met so far; the possessives, which do not decline at all; the reflexive *savo* and the ambiguity it exists to prevent; and the polite *jūs*.

rules.heading: The Personal Pronouns Declined
rules.statement: The personal pronouns have their own forms, which must be learned as a list — they follow none of the noun declensions. Three cases have now been met: the nominative for the subject (¶14), the accusative for the object (¶22), and the genitive. Observe that the third person has **one genitive for each gender**, and that *jų* serves both genders in the plural.

paradigms.caption: Personal pronouns: nominative, accusative, genitive
paradigms.footnote: *jie* is used of a mixed company; *jos* only where every member is feminine.

rules.heading: The Possessive Pronouns
rules.statement: The possessives are **mano, tavo, jo, jos, mūsų, jūsų, jų**. They are **indeclinable**: they take no ending for gender, number or case, and stand unchanged before the noun however that noun is declined. This is one of the few places where Lithuanian asks nothing of the learner. Note that in the third person and in the plural the possessive is simply the genitive of ¶42 — *jo namas* is literally "of-him house".

paradigms.caption: The possessives before a noun in three cases
paradigms.footnote: The possessive never changes; only the noun does.

rules.heading: The Reflexive Possessive Savo
rules.statement: When the possessor is **the subject of the same sentence**, Lithuanian requires **savo** in place of *jo, jos, jų*. The distinction is not a nicety: *jo* refers to somebody other than the subject, and using it where *savo* is meant says something different. English, having no such word, is ambiguous here and Lithuanian is not.

examples.note: a different man's brother — the only reading

examples.gloss: I am reading my own book.
examples.note: savo may replace mano and tavo too, where the possessor is the subject

footnotes: In the first and second persons *savo* is preferred but *mano* and *tavo* are not wrong, because no ambiguity is possible: *aš* can only be *aš*. In the third person *savo* is obligatory.

rules.heading: Jūs as the Polite Form
rules.statement: **Jūs** is both the plural "you" and the polite singular, used to one person who is a stranger, an elder, or a superior. The verb stands in the plural with it even when one person is meant. In letters it is written with a capital, *Jūs*. Using *tu* to a stranger is a real discourtesy, and the change to *tu* is something Lithuanians propose explicitly.

examples.note: to a friend or a child

rules.heading: When the Pronoun May Be Left Out
rules.statement: Because the personal ending names the person (¶24), the subject pronoun is normally **omitted** unless it is emphatic or needed to prevent confusion. Two places require it: the second conjugation, where *tu* and *jis* share the form *-i* (¶36), and the third person of every conjugation, where one form serves both numbers and both genders.

examples.gloss: I work, but she does not.
examples.note: pronouns kept because the two are contrasted

rules.heading: Tai in Naming and Introducing
rules.statement: **Tai** — this is, that is — introduces or identifies, and does not change for the gender or number of what follows. It is the word with which people and things are presented, and *yra* may be left out after it.

vocabulary.gloss: they (all feminine); also her, of her

vocabulary.notes: Indeclinable; identical to the genitive of mes.
Indeclinable; identical to the genitive of jūs.
Indeclinable; identical to the genitive of jie and jos.
Indeclinable; obligatory in the third person when the possessor is the subject.
Irregular, like vanduo; learn the genitive with the word.

drills.explanation: *mano* is the possessive and never changes. *manęs* is the genitive of the personal pronoun — "of me" as an object, not "my".
*juos*. *jas* is the accusative of the feminine *jos*, and *jų* is the genitive of both.
The possessive is indeclinable, so *mano* and *mūsų* are right before a noun in any case whatever. Only *manas* is impossible — there is no such word.

drills.stem: **Jis myli savo brolį.** What does this mean?
options: The sentence is ambiguous between the first two.
drills.explanation: *savo* points back to the subject, so the brother is his own. Had the passage meant another man's brother it would have written *jo brolį* — Lithuanian keeps apart what English leaves ambiguous.

drills.stem: You are speaking to a stranger. Which is correct?
drills.explanation: *Jūs* is the polite form and takes the plural verb *kalbate* with it, even though one person is addressed. Mixing a pronoun of one number with a verb of the other is the commonest error here.

drills.stem: In which of these sentences may the subject pronoun be dropped without loss?
drills.explanation: *dirbu* and *skaitome* name their person unmistakably. *turi* and *nori* are second-conjugation forms serving *tu*, *jis*, *ji*, *jie* and *jos* alike, so dropping the pronoun would leave the person unknown.

drills.stem: Complete: **Mes ____ nematome.** (We do not see them.)
drills.explanation: The verb is negated, so its object leaves the accusative *juos* for the genitive *jų* (¶31). The rule holds for pronouns exactly as for nouns.

drills.stem: Rūta and her sister each own a cat. **Rūta myli jos katę.** Whose cat does Rūta love?
drills.explanation: *jos* refers to somebody other than the subject, so the cat is the sister's. Rūta's own cat would require *savo katę* (¶44). English "her cat" covers both and tells you nothing.

drills.stem: Which statements about the possessives are correct?
options: They take no ending for case, gender or number.
*mūsų*, *jūsų* and *jų* are identical to the genitive of the corresponding personal pronoun.
*mano* is identical to the genitive of *aš*.
*savo* is required in the third person when the possessor is the subject.
drills.explanation: The third is the exception that proves the pattern: the genitive of *aš* is *manęs*, not *mano*. In the first and second persons the possessive and the genitive have drifted apart; in the third person and the plural they are still the same word.

drills.stem: **Aš matau tavo seserį.** How many of the four words change form if the object becomes plural, *your sisters*?
drills.explanation: One: *seserį* alone. *tavo* is indeclinable and takes no plural (¶43); *aš* and *matau* concern the subject, which has not changed. Answering two means declining the possessive, which is exactly what Lithuanian never does.

drills.title: Mano šeima
drills.passage: Labas! Mano vardas Tomas, mano pavardė Petraitis. Aš gyvenu Kaune. Tai mano šeima. Mano tėvas dirba universitete, o mano mama yra mokytoja. Aš turiu seserį. Jos vardas Eglė. Ji studijuoja Vilniuje. Eglė mėgsta savo darbą, bet nemėgsta miesto. Mes dažnai jai rašome, o ji retai rašo mums.
drills.translation: Hello! My name is Tomas, my surname is Petraitis. I live in Kaunas. This is my family. My father works at the university, and my mother is a teacher. I have a sister. Her name is Eglė. She studies in Vilnius. Eglė likes her job, but does not like the city. We often write to her, and she rarely writes to us.

questions.explanation: *mano mama yra mokytoja* — a predicate noun in the nominative (¶16). The sister studies; the mother teaches.

questions.stem: Which of these does the passage support?
questions.explanation: Eglė studies in Vilnius, not Kaunas, and it is the family who write often while she writes rarely. Note *savo darbą*: the job is her own, which is why *savo* and not *jos* stands there.

questions.stem: The passage says **Eglė mėgsta savo darbą.** If the job were her father's instead of her own, how many words would change form?
questions.explanation: One: *savo* → *jo*. Both possessives are indeclinable, so *darbą* keeps its accusative and the verb is untouched. The change is of meaning, not of form — which is the whole point of the distinction (¶44).
